one_liner: Research CUDA decompressor for standard .bz2 streams that runs every stage except parsing on the GPU; reported faster than multicore CPU bzip2.
what_it_does: Decompresses a standard bzip2 stream of up to 2^31 - 1 uncompressed bytes. Huffman/RLE2 decoding, inverse move-to-front, inverse BWT and RLE1 decoding all run on an NVIDIA GPU. The API is one static call, bz2gpu::decode_stream(host uint64_t buffer, device output pointer, output size, input size in 64-bit words, OpenMP thread count, cudaStream_t). It returns a cudaMallocAsync device buffer the caller copies back and frees. The repo ships a demo binary (bin/bz2gpu <input> <output> [gpu id]) and no library target. It only decompresses and is the companion code for an ICPP 2024 paper.
how_it_is_fast: A CPU parser finds block headers by testing every bit offset for the 48-bit block magic in parallel with OpenMP. It then builds two-level Huffman lookup tables for each block. On the GPU, Huffman and RLE2 decoding uses one thread per bzip2 block with the tables in shared memory, and zero runs become skipped writes into a pre-zeroed buffer. Inverse MTF cuts each block into 10,000-byte pieces, computes each piece's MTF permutation in parallel and joins them with a Blelloch scan over permutation composition. Inverse BWT stable-sorts the last column with CUB segmented sort to get the LF permutation, then walks it with Helman-JaJa parallel list ranking (sublist heads every 32 positions). RLE1 is undone with a parallel run-detection predicate plus a Thrust scan/scatter/gather 'expand'.
when_to_use: Bulk decompression of large existing .bz2 archives written by reference bzip2 (single stream, up to 2 GiB uncompressed each) when the next processing step runs on the GPU and can read the output from device memory.
Data-centre NVIDIA GPUs (compute capability 7.0+, A100/H100 class) with more than about 11 GB of free device memory, on Linux with CUDA 12.4.1+.
Studying or reproducing GPU inverse BWT and inverse MTF techniques (list ranking, permutation scan) from the ICPP 2024 paper.
Trusted, text-like inputs whose decompressed output you check yourself (for example against a stored hash), since the tool does not.
when_not_to_use: Untrusted or possibly corrupt archives. Block and stream CRC32s are parsed but never checked, and the parser and decoder do no bounds checks, so bad input can give silent garbage or memory corruption.
Archives from lbzip2 or pbzip2, concatenated .bz2 files, or data with runs of small byte values. The RLE1 stage can mis-decode these (see gotchas).

Streams over 2^31 - 1 uncompressed bytes (no batching). Small archives: Huffman decoding uses one GPU thread per 900 kB block, so few blocks leave the GPU mostly idle, and the inverse-BWT buffers are a fixed ~10 GB allocation whatever the input size.
GPUs with less than ~12 GB of memory, non-NVIDIA hardware, Windows or macOS.
Any need for compression, streaming, a stable library API or production support. The README says it 'is not suitable for production use'; the repo has 2 commits and no tests.

integration.dependencies: CUDA Toolkit 12.4.1+ (CUB and Thrust from the toolkit; src/rle.cu and include/thrust_custom_alloc.cuh hold modified Thrust code under Apache-2.0 with LLVM exceptions), OpenMP (libgomp), std::filesystem (-lstdc++fs)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; GCC 11.4.1+; CUDA SDK 12.4.1+; GPU compute capability 7.0+ (README). The Makefile builds with -O3 -arch=native -march=native.
integration.platforms: NVIDIA GPUs (cc 7.0+) on GNU/Linux. The host side is built with -march=native for the build machine. Other host architectures are not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. decode_stream takes a caller-supplied cudaStream_t, but the parser calls omp_set_num_threads() process-wide, and any CUDA error (including out-of-memory) calls exit(1) through the CUERR macro.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: reads the standard .bz2 format but is not a bzip2/libbz2 replacement. It has a different C++ API and a demo CLI (input, output, GPU id), decompresses only, offers no streaming, and does not verify checksums.

gotchas: Likely RLE1 correctness bug, found from a Python port and not run on a GPU. is_run in src/rle.cu decides whether a byte is a run-length count from the 9 bytes before it only (preceded_by_run plus a backward parity chain), not from decoder state. The port gets 'a'x101 + 'b'x102 + 'c' wrong: 'c' is read as a count and becomes 99 extra 'b's. It also fails on 0x01x5 + 0x00x4 + 0x03 and on any run of 511 or more 0xFB bytes. It produced 18 and 50 false count bytes per MB on synthetic 8-bit low-value image and label-map data, but none on ELF binaries (ls, bash, libc), small-int64 arrays or JSON text. Because CRCs are never checked, the wrong output goes unreported.

RLE1 runs on all blocks concatenated, so a run split across a block boundary is decoded as one run. Reference bzip2 never splits a run across blocks within one stream: its pending run carries into the next block. lbzip2 does split runs: its encode.c collect() ends a full block mid-run. pbzip2 and cat'd .bz2 files are multi-stream, and the parser's block-magic scan accepts them silently. In the port, a 4-space indent split 2+2 across two streams turned the following 'r' into 114 spaces, and 89 of 2000 random cut points in a Python source file decoded wrong.

Memory: batch_iBWT allocates buffers for 800 blocks whatever the input size. At -9 (900 kB blocks) that is 2 x 720 MB of keys plus 3 x 2.88 GB of uint32 arrays, about 10.3 GB, even for the 10 MB test file. RLE1 then adds about 2 GB of Thrust buffers. The compressed input and the full output must also fit on the device.

No bitstream validation. A selector MTF index at or above the tree count writes past a host std::vector in parse_selectors. A tree count of 7 overflows the 6-table code_lengths slot, and decode_block never bounds out_idx. Randomised blocks (bzip2 0.9.0) are not handled (the flag is skipped). The block size is read once from the first stream header. The block finder reads one uint64 past the input buffer, and the API input size is in 64-bit words, not bytes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over lbzip2 (the catalogued multi-threaded bzip2: 62.7 vs 41.1 MB/s single-thread decompression in lzbench 2.4) only to decompress large reference-bzip2 archives on a data-centre GPU, keep the output on the device, and check the output yourself. lbzip2 verifies CRCs, has no size limit and handles multi-stream files. For new data, zstd or libbsc (both catalogued) are better format choices than any bzip2 decoder.
verified_claims_summary: The repo has no benchmark or timing code (the timer macros in include/helpers.h are unused). All figures come from an unreproduced search snippet of the ICPP 2024 paper: up to 6.1x over an unnamed multicore CPU implementation for the inverse-BWT stage alone, up to 2400 MB/s for inverse BWT plus inverse MTF on an A100, and over 11.62 GB/s bzip2 decompression on a DGX H100. A DGX H100 is an 8-GPU server and the demo uses one GPU. Not documented: whether that figure is aggregate, whether it includes host transfers and the CPU parser, and the CPU model, baseline program or compiler flags behind any of the numbers.
status_note: Stale research artifact (2 commits, 2024-07-15 and 2024-07-16; 6 stars, 0 forks, no issues, no tests); MIT with Apache-2.0 Thrust-derived files, so copyable for study, but it should not be used as a production decompressor: it skips CRC checks and the RLE1 stage likely mis-decodes some inputs.
